title: Evacuation behaviour and vulnerable-population parameters for the California scenario engine
units: shares are fractions in [0, 1]; times are minutes unless stated; clock times are local (Pacific) as published
evidence_rule: status is one of: sourced (value read from the cited document), derived (arithmetic on sourced values, shown in 'derivation'), assumption (no source; a placeholder for sensitivity runs, not a finding), gap (no usable source found; value is null). A sourced range keeps its published low and high; 'suggested' is our pick inside it and is an assumption unless stated.
caveats: Most numbers come from convenience-sample surveys (online, shelters) with sampling bias; Wong et al. and Kuligowski et al. both warn of this. Survey evacuation rates run above GPS-inferred rates (Kincade: about 80% survey vs 46% GPS inside zones).
Camp Fire (2018) was a no-notice, fast-moving event; Tubbs, Thomas, Carr and Kincade gave more warning. Do not mix their delay distributions without saying which is which.
Australian figures are stated intentions to a hypothetical scenario or a different policy regime (stay and defend); they bound the 'wait and see' share, they do not measure California behaviour.

wong2020.citation: Wong, S.D., Broader, J.C., Shaheen, S.A. (2020). Review of California Wildfire Evacuations from 2017 to 2019. UC Institute of Transportation Studies research report. DOI 10.7922/G29G5K2R.
wong2020.kind: online survey, Oct 2017 N. California fires (Tubbs, Nuns, Atlas; n=79), Dec 2017 S. California fires (Thomas, Creek, Skirball; n=226), 2018 Carr Fire (n=284)

grajdura2022.citation: Grajdura, S. (2022). Mixed Methods Approaches to Wildfire Evacuation: Modeling Behavior, Simulation, and Equity. PhD dissertation, UC Davis. Survey results first published in Grajdura, Qian, Niemeier (2021), Awareness, departure, and preparation time in no-notice wildfire evacuations, Safety Science 139:105258.
grajdura2022.kind: Camp Fire survey, 2 to 6 weeks after the fire, Red Cross shelters (133) and online (264), n=397; 26 shelter interviews; Butte County CodeRED logs (FOIA)

zhao2022.citation: Zhao, X., Xu, Y., Lovreglio, R., Kuligowski, E., Nilsson, D., Cova, T., Wu, A., Yan, X. Estimating wildfire evacuation decision and departure timing using large-scale GPS data (2019 Kincade Fire, Sonoma County). arXiv:2109.07745; published in Transportation Research Part D (2022).
zhao2022.kind: GPS panel (5,166 inferred homes) for the 2019 Kincade Fire

kuligowski2022.citation: Kuligowski, E.D., Zhao, X., Lovreglio, R., Xu, N., Yang, K., Westbury, A., Nilsson, D., Brown, N. Modeling evacuation decisions in the 2019 Kincade fire in California. Safety Science (2022). Author manuscript read.
kuligowski2022.kind: online survey of Sonoma County households, n=270

nist2252.citation: Maranghides, A., et al. (2023). A Case Study of the Camp Fire: Notification, Evacuation, Traffic, and Temporary Refuge Areas. NIST Technical Note 2252, July 2023. DOI 10.6028/NIST.TN.2252.
nist2252.kind: reconstruction from 911, radio and interview data; no resident survey
nist2252.licence: NIST technical note, US government work (public domain in the US)

mclennan2014.citation: McLennan, J., Elliott, G., Wright, L. (2014). Bushfire survival preparations by householders in at-risk areas of south-eastern Australia. Australian Journal of Emergency Management 29(2).
mclennan2014.kind: survey of n=584 householders in at-risk communities asked what they would do if told a fire would reach them in 1 to 2 hours (hypothetical)

whittaker2013.citation: Whittaker, J., Haynes, K., Handmer, J., McLennan, J. (2013). Community safety during the 2009 Australian 'Black Saturday' bushfires: an analysis of household preparedness and response. International Journal of Wildland Fire 22(6):841-849.
whittaker2013.kind: mail survey n=1,314 and 600+ interviews, Black Saturday 2009
whittaker2013.note: Abstract-level only: the full text was not read. Use as a pointer, not as a parameter source.

acs2022.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2018-2022 5-Year Estimates, tables B25044, B01001, B18101, C16002.

assumption.citation: No source. Placeholder chosen by the authors of this file for sensitivity runs.

parameters.description: Share of households that received a mandatory evacuation order and evacuated.
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 11 (p. 39); text p. 38 gives non-compliance 3.2% to 13.0%
parameters.n: n=79, 226, 284 (all respondents; order recipients are a subset)
parameters.comparison: Differs: demand.py sends 100% of households in noticed block groups by car. The survey range implies 3% to 13% do not leave. The GPS panel for Kincade gives a much lower 46% inside warning/order zones (Zhao et al., Sec. 4.4.3, p. 18) because it counts 'stayed' for everyone not seen leaving; use it as a pessimistic bound.

parameters.description: Share of Camp Fire survey respondents who reported receiving an evacuation order at any time on 2018-11-08.
parameters.locator: Grajdura 2022, Ch. 3 text p. 37 (19%); Figure 4 caption text p. 38 gives 21% 'official notification'
parameters.n: n=397 (not every question has a full n)
parameters.comparison: The Camp record is mostly cue-driven: only 1.3% (5 of 397) first learned of the fire from an official notice, 44.6% saw it themselves, 26.3% were told in person, 17.1% call or text, 6.9% online, 3.8% TV or radio (Table 12, p. 103). The sim's order trigger therefore explains little of Camp; its fire and social cues carry the load, which matches.

parameters.description: Camp Fire timing: first awareness, official CodeRED, departure. Local time on 2018-11-08.
parameters.derivation: mean awareness-to-departure gap = 09:33 - 08:00 = 93 min (difference of two sample means; the paper shows a 'very short gap' for early risers, p. 39). Among respondents aware before 08:55 the mean departure is 09:13 (regression-tree leaf near Figure 7, p. 70).
parameters.locator: Grajdura 2022, pp. 51-52 (awareness SD 71 min, mean 8:00, mean departure 9:33, median 9:00, CodeRED cluster 9:11); p. 39 (short gap); p. 70 (regression-tree leaf)
parameters.n: n=397; 98% gave awareness time, 99% departure time
parameters.sim_value: order: decision median 21 min + prep median 15 min (mean about 48 min total); warning only: decision median 83 min + prep (mean about 138 min); fire cue: decision median 7 min + prep (mean about 28 min)
parameters.comparison: Camp's mean gap of about 93 min sits between the sim's order (about 48 min) and warning-only (about 138 min) cases. That is consistent with a population mostly unordered but seeing fire. It is not a calibration: the sim has not been fit to this.

parameters.description: Adjustments to the awareness-to-departure delay estimated for Camp Fire respondents (ceteris paribus regression).
parameters.locator: Grajdura 2022, p. 53 (men +23 min, insured homeowners +34 min), p. 52 (15+ years' tenure 'upwards of half an hour'), p. 48 (age 65 and over about 34 minutes later awareness)
parameters.comparison: The sim has no covariates. If the residents generator assigns age, tenure or tenure type, these effects can scale prep time per agent. Effects are regression coefficients with wide intervals.

parameters.description: Kincade Fire GPS panel: share of all evacuees by trigger.
parameters.unit: fraction of evacuees (rounding: sums to 1.01 as published)
parameters.locator: Zhao et al., Sec. 4.4.1, p. 16 and Figure 10
parameters.sim_param: social_hazard_per_h and fire_cue_hazard_per_h (no explicit pre-notice share)
parameters.comparison: Over half of evacuees (self plus shadow, 55%) left without an order for them. The sim only creates demand in zones with an order or warning (demand.py), so shadow evacuation is absent. 7% left as soon as a warning arrived; the sim's warning-only hazard (0.5/h, median 83 min) is much slower than that. Kincade residents had lived through Tubbs (2017), so this mix is a high-sensitivity case.

parameters.description: Share of households that did NOT receive a mandatory order and evacuated anyway.
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 11 (p. 39), text p. 38-39
parameters.n: non-recipient cells are small; the paper does not print cell counts
parameters.sim_param: none (no evacuation without a notice in a zone with no order)
parameters.comparison: Gap in the sim. Wong et al. note one explanation is that officials could not issue orders before residents needed to leave. Suggested use: a share of households in unordered block groups within a buffer of the fire evacuates on the fire or social cue.

suggested.note: low end of the range; the 75% (Carr) comes from a fire with a 2-day build-up and likely over-states unordered behaviour for a fast fire

parameters.description: Share of all survey respondents who evacuated.
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 10 (p. 37); Kuligowski et al. results text (79% decided to evacuate; 80% evacuated)
parameters.comparison: Differs for the same reason as order_compliance; the Oct 2017 sample is mostly non-evacuees (53.2%).

parameters.description: Stated intention if told a bushfire would reach the home in 1 to 2 hours: leave at once, stay and defend, wait and see.
parameters.locator: McLennan, Elliott and Wright 2014, results text: 273 (47%) leave, 139 (24%) stay and defend, 172 (29%) wait and see, of 584
parameters.comparison: Differs: sim holds out 7% who ignore notices until they see fire, against 29% 'wait and see' plus 24% 'stay and defend' stated in Australia. Intentions overstate staying in a policy that encourages it, and California shows 3% to 13% non-compliance among ordered households (Wong), so 7% is inside the observed non-compliance range. Keep 0.07 as the baseline and run 0.13 as the upper bound.
parameters.pointer: Whittaker et al. 2013 (Black Saturday, n=1,314) reports about half of respondents stayed to defend; abstract-level only, not used as a parameter.

parameters.description: Non-evacuees who gave 'wanted to protect property' as a reason (multiple answers allowed).
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 20 (p. 51)
parameters.comparison: Supports 'stay and defend' as a minority motive; with non-evacuation of 10.6% to 53.2% of respondents, 17% to 37% of those is about 2% to 20% of all respondents.

parameters.description: Departure hour of day among evacuees (local time).
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 10 (p. 37)
parameters.sim_param: none (the sim clocks decisions from notices and cues, not the time of day)
parameters.comparison: Context only: these fires started or surged at night, which Camp (06:15 start) did not. Camp's daytime profile is in camp_awareness_departure_timing.

parameters.description: Personal vehicles a household used to evacuate.
parameters.unit: fraction of evacuees (shares of all evacuees; the remainder used rental, RV, trailer, walking and similar)
parameters.derivation: Mean vehicles among personal-vehicle users, counting 'more than two' as 3: 1.72, 1.61, 1.82. Counting it as 2 (the sim's cap): 1.58, 1.52, 1.65.
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 10 'Mode Choice' (p. 38); executive summary p. 5 gives 34% to 45% one vehicle and 49% to 62% two or more
parameters.comparison: Close. For Butte, min(vehicles available, 2) averages 1.69 over vehicle-owning households (from tools/people_acs_butte_fixture.json: 24,535 / 31,350 / 22,371 households with 1 / 2 / 3+ vehicles), against 1.52 to 1.65 observed with the same cap. The sim is 2% to 11% high, within survey noise. The cap of 2 truncates the 9% to 17% who took three or more.

parameters.description: Survey households with pets.
parameters.unit: fraction of respondent households (convenience sample, likely above the population share)
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table A1 household characteristics (p. 61)
parameters.comparison: Gap in the sim: no pets. Pets are a stated reason for 7.1% to 10.0% of non-evacuees ('not sure where pets could be taken'; Table 20, p. 51). NIST TN 2252 records civilians with pets and livestock at refuge areas until 15:30 (Sec. 9, TRA-W description, p. 144) and the pre-fire evacuation plan had pet provisions (p. 30).

parameters.description: Extra preparation time for a household with pets or livestock.
parameters.locator: none. Kuligowski et al. 2022 find pets or livestock correlate negatively with evacuation (r = -0.137 with risk perception) but give no minutes.
parameters.comparison: No source for the size of the effect. Use only in sensitivity runs and label it.

parameters.description: Residents trying to return into the zone while it is closed or still burning.
parameters.locator: none found. Related, sourced: 91.9% to 96.9% of evacuees eventually returned home (Wong Table 10, p. 38); 3% to 32% returned two weeks or more after the outbreak (executive summary p. 5); 0% to 3.3% of non-evacuees 'tried to leave but went back home due to traffic' (Table 20, p. 51).
parameters.sim_param: turn_back_prob (a different concept: turning around on a blocked edge)
parameters.comparison: turn_back_prob has no published counterpart. Return attempts during an order are not quantified in the documents read; an after-action report or CHP closure-breach count would be needed.

parameters.description: Share of evacuees who later returned to their home.
parameters.locator: Wong et al. 2020, Table 10 'Returned Home' (p. 38)
parameters.comparison: Not a Camp number: Carr and the 2017 fires burned far fewer homes than Camp (about 18,800 structures destroyed), so Camp's rate will be lower.

parameters.description: Households with no vehicle available, Butte County, ACS 2018-2022.
parameters.derivation: 5,063 / 83,319 households summed over the 200 block groups in tools/people_acs_butte_fixture.json (B25044 cells 3 and 10 over cell 1). Block-group shares vary and carry a 90% margin; read them per block group.
parameters.sim_param: demand.py counts households with no vehicle but does not convert them to vehicles
parameters.comparison: Same treatment: the residents generator should hold them as carless, to be picked up (transit, neighbours, responders).

parameters.description: Population aged 65 and over, Butte County, ACS 2018-2022.
parameters.derivation: 38,852 / 213,605 over 200 block groups (B01001 cells 20-25 and 44-49 over cell 1).
parameters.comparison: Context. Paradise-area block groups run near 33% in this vintage.

parameters.description: People with a disability, Butte County, ACS 2018-2022 (tract level).
parameters.derivation: 34,705 / 211,587: sum over the 54 tracts of with-disability over civilian noninstitutionalized population (B18101). B18101 has no block-group rows; the extract repeats each tract's counts on its block groups. Survey households with a member with a disability: 14.2% to 19.0% (Wong Table A1, p. 61).
parameters.locator: ACS B18101; Wong et al. 2020 p. 61
parameters.comparison: Not in sim. Disability is a population share, not a household-needs-help share: how many need physical assistance is not in these tables.

parameters.description: Limited English speaking households, Butte County, ACS 2018-2022.
parameters.derivation: 1,859 / 83,319 households (C16002 cells 4, 7, 10, 13 over cell 1) summed over 200 block groups.
parameters.comparison: Could scale a notification-miss or delay factor for English-only alerts; no published effect size was found (gap).

parameters.description: Share of Camp Fire entrapment, assistance and rescue (EA/R) events that involved a person with a pre-existing condition (medical, mobility, or no vehicle or unable to drive).
parameters.derivation: 59 of 198 events; NIST says the real figure is higher because the information was not recorded for all events. 5 of the 59 were fatal, and 5 of the 6 fatal events involved a pre-existing condition.
parameters.comparison: Use as an outcome check for a vulnerable-resident model: at least 30% of Camp rescues involved such a person.

parameters.description: Camp Fire survey respondents without a smartphone, and respondents who needed several modes to leave.
parameters.locator: Grajdura 2022, Table 12 (p. 103: 85.9% own, 14.1% do not); p. 74 (at least 7% needed more than one mode: a stranger's vehicle, police vehicle, walking)
parameters.comparison: Context for a vulnerable-resident model and for vehicle abandonment on the road.

parameters.description: B-Line (Butte Regional Transit) buses in the Camp Fire evacuation.

value.normal_service: two fixed routes from Chico plus seven Paratransit buses stationed in Paradise
value.first_dispatch_clock: 09:00 (three large and two Paratransit buses to Butte College)

parameters.locator: NIST TN 2252, Sec. 9.3.3 (pp. 153-154), Table 36 (p. 154), Appendix J; p. 153 (convoy to carry civilians without vehicles)
parameters.comparison: Transit capacity arrived at about 17:00, 9 hours after the fire reached Paradise, for people already at refuge areas. A scenario can set a bus pickup event with these timings; the B-Line GTFS feed (stops, routes) is a separate gap listed in docs/people-data.md.

parameters.description: Camp Fire facility evacuation examples.

feather_river_hospital.vehicles: staff cars, law enforcement vehicles, ambulances; two ambulances entrapped in a burnover on Pentz Road after 09:00; about 160 civilians later sheltered at the hospital refuge area for over 6 hours

cypress_meadows_post_acute.vehicles: staff and law enforcement vehicles; some patients stuck in gridlock and sheltered at a refuge area

value.paradise_care_facilities: at least 20 facilities, from in-home care with under 10 beds to over 130 beds
value.schools: evacuated by an unknown number of school buses and staff cars; students without transport were picked up by Paradise Police

parameters.locator: NIST TN 2252, Sec. 7.3 (pp. 79-82), Table 14 (p. 81)
parameters.comparison: Facility evacuations are outside the traffic model today. Scenario inputs can use these as examples of lead time (Cypress Meadows needed more than 2 hours for half its patients) and of vehicle sources (staff and police cars, ambulances).

gaps: No quantified departure-delay distribution after an order or warning for Tubbs, Thomas, Kincade or Australian fires was obtainable: the survey papers report timing by clock hour or by day, not minutes after a message. Camp (Grajdura) is the only minutes-scale source and it is mostly cue-driven.
Return attempts into a closed or burning zone: no published rate found.
Pet and livestock effect on delay: no published minutes.
Effect of limited English or disability on notification delay: no published size.
B-Line GTFS (stops, routes, 2018 schedule) not downloaded: the current Mobility Database feed has no licence text and covers 2026 service, not 2018.
